problem: Classical image-based visual servoing is brittle (needs reliable sparse features, depth, and enough view overlap), and prior learned locomotion/target-reaching policies (siamese, stacked-image, attention-based) generalize poorly and mostly target semantic objects rather than goal views.
motivation: Visual servoing is a local navigation skill for view-based topological navigation, and it should work without calibration or depth across environments and targets. Dense correspondence between current and goal views is the quantity classical IBVS uses, so feeding it to a learned policy with a control-error-inspired reward should give a view- and target-invariant controller.
key_idea: Train a DQN policy whose input is the dense x/y correspondence-offset map between current and goal views, with a reward based on normalized reduction of a polar-pose distance, so the policy is invariant to appearance and target type.
insight: Feeding dense correspondence rather than raw image pairs is what generalizes: correspondence map gives 85.7/80.3% (short/long range) vs 26.5/18.2% for LocomotionNet and 14.3/28.8% for SiameseNet, and smoothing improves it to 90.9/86.9%. The reward ablation shows the DistMinimize reward with d_polar (83.5%) beats the Progress reward with d_polar (73.2%) and with d_pose (54.9%). The learned policy is also robust to noisy or missing correspondences and continues moving when the goal view overlap is lost, where IBVS stops.
method: Problem setup: the agent gets a start view and a goal view with some overlap, and outputs discrete actions (0.1 m forward in 7 headings: ±π/4, ±π/6, ±π/15, 0). No calibration or depth is used at test time apart from computing the correspondences.

Input representation: a two-channel dense correspondence map (per-pixel x/y offsets from the current view to the goal view), currently computed from GT pose and depth. Smoothing is applied at test time to reduce depth discontinuities and sparsity.
Perception module: 4 conv layers (5x5x16, 3x3x32, 3x3x64, each with ReLU, batch norm and max pool, then a 1x1 conv) giving a 16x16x1 feature map.
Action module: the flattened 256-d vector goes to an FC layer that outputs Q-values for the 7 actions. An LSTM was tried and gave no gain.
Reward: R = max(0, min(d_{t-1}/d_init,1) − min(d_t/d_init,1)), with d_polar = ρ + λα|α| + λβ|β| (λ=0.2), motivated by the differential-drive feedback control error.
Training: DQN with replay memory, minibatch 128, RMSprop, lr 1e-5, 50k iterations (~6 h on a single GPU), 16 Gibson training scenes.
Target-object servoing: an off-the-shelf detector (Mask R-CNN) crops the object from images collected while roaming, and the crop is used as the target image (qualitative only).

setting.backbone: Small 4-layer CNN + FC DQN (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: 16 Gibson scenes with random start poses and target views 0.5-4 m away, heading within ±π/4 (5-35 steps per episode); no extra data
setting.observation: Dense correspondence map between the current RGB view and the goal view image (computed from GT pose and depth); RGB/RGB-D images
setting.action_space: 7 discrete actions: move forward 0.1 m at headings from -π/4 to π/4
setting.privileged: GT pose and depth used to compute the dense correspondences (both train and test); GT pose used for the reward in training

numbers_note: No standard benchmark (R2R, ObjectNav etc.) is used; the results come from the authors' own Gibson setup. Noise-robustness results are given only in a figure (text: ~80% at 32 px offset noise, >75% with 50% missing correspondences).
results: The LVS policy with smoothed dense correspondence reaches 90.9% (short) and 86.9% (long-range) success, far above LocomotionNet (26.5/18.2%) and SiameseNet (14.3/28.8%). It also beats the best classical IBVS variant with GT sparse correspondences and GT depth (80.4/72.2/80.4%) by at least 8% on textured and nontextured scenes, without needing depth.
limitations: Dense correspondences are computed from GT pose and depth in simulation, so the method has not been shown with learned correspondences, and there is no real-robot validation.
Evaluation is small (6 test scenes, ~10 starts each), without obstacles, and only with a dense reward; object-target servoing is qualitative only.
Requires overlap between the start and goal view, and the policy is purely reactive (no gain from an LSTM).
